translationRepairs: Ji Rong of Liaodong cowed the northern tribes until his name carried across the sea; Hui, Mo, Wa, and Korea all sent envoys from immense distances, and from the Zhanghe and Yonghe eras onward diplomatic traffic never stopped.

Ji Rong of Liaodong cowed the northern tribes until his name carried across the sea; Hui, Mo, Wa, and Han all sent envoys from immense distances, and from the reigns of Emperors Zhang and He onward diplomatic traffic never stopped.
章、和 matches the emperor-pair pattern of 桓、靈 in the next sentences, not the era names Zhanghe or Yonghe; 韓 is the Han peoples of this treatise, not a general 'Korea'.

At that time the Liaodong governor Ji Rong awed the north with his might; his reputation reached beyond the seas; thereupon the Hui, Mo, Wa, and Han, from ten thousand li away, came to court with offerings; therefore after the Zhanghe and Yonghe reigns, embassies flowed without cease.

At that time the Liaodong governor Ji Rong awed the north with his might; his reputation reached beyond the seas; thereupon the Hui, Mo, Wa, and Han, from ten thousand li away, came to court with offerings; therefore after Emperors Zhang and He, embassies flowed without cease.
The literal line wrongly treats 章、和 as reign titles Zhanghe and Yonghe; they are Emperors Zhang and He, after whose time 使聘流通.
Long ago Yao posted Xi Zhong to Wuyi at Yang Valley, the place where legend places the sunrise.
Long ago Yao ordered Xi Zhong to reside at Yu-yi, called Yang Valley, the place where the sun is said to rise.
命…宅 is an order to dwell at 嵎夷, which the text names 旸谷; the original turns that identification into a posting 'to Wuyi at' a second site.
Once King Mu had fine steppe horses, he sent Zaofu at the reins to alert Chu and ordered a strike on Xu—the ride took a single day.
After King Mu obtained teams of Ji and Lu steeds, he had Zaofu drive to inform Chu and ordered an attack on Xu, arriving in a single day.
骥騄之乘 are named swift-horse teams obtained later (後得), not generic steppe horses introduced by 'once'.
The king considered him divine and then listened to the mother to raise him; his name was Dongming.
The king considered him divine and then allowed the mother to raise him; his name was Dongming.
听母收養 is permission for the mother to rear the child, not listening to her advice; the idiomatic line already has this sense.
Dongming grew up skilled at archery; the king envied his fierceness and again wished to kill him.
Dongming grew up skilled at archery; the king feared his fierceness and again wished to kill him.
忌其猛 is wary fear of Dongming's fierceness, which motivates 復欲殺之; 'envied' invents jealousy.
Jianwu 32 brought tribute envoys; Emperor Guangwu restored the Koguryŏ king's rank.
In the eighth year of Jianwu, Koguryŏ sent tribute envoys; Emperor Guangwu restored its king's title.
建武八年 is Jianwu year 8, not a label 'Jianwu 32'; the original also drops 高句驪 as the tribute sender.
That winter more than ten thousand people led by the chief Dai Sheng of the Can branch tribe surrendered to Han authorities at Lelang.
In the winter of the twenty-third year, Gouli's Can-branch elder Dai Sheng and others, more than ten thousand people, went to Lelang and submitted internally.
'That winter' wrongly ties 二十三年冬 to Jianwu 8; the proposed wording is accurate but needs Gouli's as a possessive so Can-branch elder is grammatical.
In spring of Jianwu 49 they struck four commanderies until Ji Rong of Liaodong coaxed them back to allegiance at the frontier.

In spring of the twenty-fifth year, Gouli raided Youbeiping, Yuyang, Shanggu, and Taiyuan, until Liaodong governor Ji Rong summoned them with grace and trust; all again submitted at the barrier passes.
二十五年春 is Jianwu year 25, not year 49; the original also omits the four named commanderies and 皆復款塞.
In spring of Yuanxing 1 (105 CE) they swept into Liaodong and ravaged six counties until Prefect Geng Kui routed them and killed their leader.
In spring of Yuanxing 1 (AD 105) under Emperor He they again swept into Liaodong and ravaged six counties until Prefect Geng Kui routed them and beheaded their chieftain.
The original omits 和帝 and 復 and weakens 斬其渠帥 to 'killed'; the proposal is right on substance but needlessly replaces already accurate idiomatic verbs.
Closing Chen Zhong's memorial, Emperor An approved.
安帝从之 only says Emperor An followed the advice; 'Closing Chen Zhong's memorial' is not in this sentence.
Between Emperors Zhi and Huan they struck Xi'anping in Liaodong, murdered the Daifang prefect, and carried off the Lelang governor's family.
Between Emperors Zhi and Huan they struck Xi'anping in Liaodong, murdered the Daifang magistrate, and carried off the Lelang governor's wife and children.
帶方令 is a county magistrate, not a prefect; 妻子 is the governor's wife and children, not a vague 'family'.
Shiyuan 5 (86 BCE) abolished Lintun and Zhenfan and merged them into Lelang and Xuantu.
Shiyuan 5 (82 BCE) abolished Lintun and Zhenfan and merged them into Lelang and Xuantu.
昭帝始元五年 is Shiyuan 5 of Emperor Zhao, 82 BCE; 86 BCE is Shiyuan 1.
Byeonjin lies south of Jinhan with another dozen states fronting Japan.
Byeonjin lies south of Jinhan with another dozen states fronting Wa.
其南亦與倭接 names Wa, the same ethnonym used in the adjoining sentences; 'Japan' is anachronistic.
Near Japan to the south some practice tattooing.
Near Wa to the south some practice tattooing.
其南界近倭 names Wa, not Japan.
Jianwu 44 brought envoys such as Su Ma-di of the Liansi Han to Lelang with gifts.
In the twentieth year of Jianwu (AD 44), Han people such as Su Ma-di of Liansi went to Lelang with tribute.
建武二十年 is Jianwu year 20 (AD 44), not 'Jianwu 44'; 韓人廉斯人苏馬諟 is a Liansi man among the Han, not a polity called Liansi Han.
From Lelang's frontier to Wa is twelve thousand li; Kuyegan on Wa's northwest lies seven thousand li beyond.
From the Lelang commandery frontier to their country is twelve thousand li, and to Kuyegan, their northwest border, more than seven thousand li.
Both versions misread 去其西北界拘邪韓國: the Lelang frontier is 12,000 li from Wa and 7,000-odd li from Kuyegan, which is Wa's northwest bound, not a further leg from that bound.
Under Emperors Huan and Ling Japan fell into war without a king for years.
Under Emperors Huan and Ling, the state of Wa fell into great disorder and mutual attacks, remaining without a ruler for years.
倭國大亂，更相攻伐，历年無主 is disorder and mutual attacks in the state of Wa, not 'Japan fell into war'; the original English does not fuse 'Ling Japan', but Japan and the omitted clauses are still wrong.
A shaman-queen named Himiko, unmarried in age, bewitched the people into making her ruler.
There was a woman named Himiko, advanced in years and unmarried, who served the way of ghosts and spirits; able to bewitch the crowd with sorcery, they together established her as ruler.
The source has a woman 卑弥呼, 年長不嫁, who 事鬼神道 and is then 共立為王; 'shaman-queen' and 'unmarried in age' are invented or unintelligible, and 事鬼神道 is omitted.
Four thousand li south stands Zhuru, whose people stand three or four feet tall.
More than four thousand li south of the queen's state is Zhuru, whose people are three or four chi tall.
The distance is 自女王國南四千餘里, and stature is 三四尺, Han chi, not English feet.
Legend makes Xu Fu's failed quest for Penglai end on these isles, where his thousands of colonists multiplied into myriads.

Tradition says Qin Shi Huang sent the fangshi Xu Fu with several thousand boys and girls to sea in search of the Penglai immortals; failing, Xu Fu feared execution, dared not return, and settled on this island, where successive generations came to number tens of thousands of households.
The sentence is the Xu Fu legend in full: 秦始皇遣方士徐福 with 童男女, failure at Penglai, 畏誅不敢還, settlement, and 數萬家 by 世世相承.
That is the essence of how sages frame law—sparse statutes grounded in trust."
If, like Jizi, one trims the statutes and relies on good faith, one touches the very root from which the sages fashioned law!"
The judgment is explicitly 若箕子; dropping Jizi turns a comparison to him into a free-floating maxim.
